trails.name: The Freedom Trail
trails.summary: Two and a half miles of red brick through sixteen Revolutionary sites, from Boston Common to the Bunker Hill Monument. The line is painted and inlaid into the pavement, so you cannot get lost, and you can join or leave it anywhere.

stops.name: Boston Common
stops.desc: Where the trail starts, and America's oldest public park. Militia drilled here, cows grazed here until 1830, and the redcoats camped here before Lexington.

stops.name: Massachusetts State House
stops.desc: The gold dome above the Common, finished 1798 on John Hancock's cow pasture. The dome was wood, then copper rolled by Paul Revere, and it is gold leaf now.
stops.yiki: Stand across the street and look straight up. In the Second World War they painted the dome grey so it would not shine for bombers off the coast. It is gold again now, and on a clear morning you have to squint.

stops.name: Park Street Church
stops.desc: The corner was once the town granary, then a powder store in 1812, which is why locals called it Brimstone Corner. America Is My Country was first sung here in 1831.
stops.yiki: Pick out the tall white steeple from a few streets away. For years it was the first thing a traveler saw riding into Boston, so you can arrive at it the way they did.

stops.name: Granary Burying Ground
stops.desc: Samuel Adams, John Hancock, Paul Revere and the five who died in the Boston Massacre are all in this one small yard. The headstones were rearranged for lawnmowers, so the stones and the graves no longer match.
stops.yiki: Find the tall obelisk in the centre. It marks Benjamin Franklin's mother and father, though Franklin himself lies in Philadelphia. Read a few of the winged skulls while you are here, the carving softens as the century turns.

stops.name: King's Chapel
stops.desc: The first Anglican church in Puritan Boston, deeply unwelcome, so it was built around the old wooden one and the timber was thrown out the windows. The bell is Revere's largest.
stops.yiki: Notice the tower stops square and plain. The steeple it was drawn for was never built, the money ran out, and Bostonians rather grew to like it unfinished. Inside, the high box pews were rented by the family.

stops.name: Boston Latin School site
stops.desc: The first public school in America, 1635. Benjamin Franklin went here and did not graduate. His statue stands on the spot.
stops.yiki: Look down, not up. The schoolhouse is long gone, and the spot is a mosaic set into the pavement. Several signers of the Declaration learned their Latin here before Franklin did, and left better credentialed than he managed to.

stops.name: Old Corner Bookstore
stops.desc: The oldest commercial building downtown, 1718, and the publishing house that printed Hawthorne, Emerson, Longfellow and Stowe. It is a Chipotle now, which locals will tell you about at length.
stops.yiki: It was nearly a parking lot. A handful of Bostonians bought the building in nineteen sixty to stop the wreckers, and that one fight started the group that has since saved a good deal of what you will walk past today.

stops.name: Old South Meeting House
stops.desc: Five thousand colonists packed in here on 16 December 1773, could not get the tea sent back, and walked out to the harbour. The Tea Party started in this room.
stops.yiki: When the British held the town they tore out the pews and rode horses inside, to insult the very room where it had started. Stand in the middle and picture it packed to the walls, because on that December night it was.

stops.name: Old State House
stops.desc: The oldest surviving public building in Boston, 1713, with the lion and unicorn still on the gable. The Declaration of Independence was read from that balcony in 1776 and is read from it every Fourth of July.
stops.yiki: The lion and the unicorn are the crown's own animals, and in seventeen seventy six the crowd pulled the first pair down and burned them in the street. These are later copies, put back once the anger had cooled. A subway runs directly under the floor now.

stops.name: Boston Massacre Site
stops.desc: A ring of cobblestones in a traffic island. Five men died here on 5 March 1770, and John Adams defended the soldiers in court because he thought the trial mattered more than the verdict.
stops.yiki: Mind the traffic to reach it, then look back up at the balcony above you, because the two places are one story. The first of the five to fall was Crispus Attucks, a sailor of African and Wampanoag descent.

stops.name: Faneuil Hall
stops.desc: The meeting hall where the argument for revolution was made out loud, 1742, with the grasshopper weather vane still on top. Food stalls downstairs, the hall itself upstairs and free.

stops.name: Paul Revere House
stops.desc: The oldest house in downtown Boston, about 1680, and he owned it on the night of the ride. Small, dark, low ceilings, and the most convincing room on the whole trail.
stops.yiki: Duck your head, the doorways were built for smaller people. He raised a large family in these few rooms across two marriages, and the tightness of the place tells you more about the man than any label on the wall.

stops.name: Old North Church
stops.desc: One if by land, two if by sea. The two lanterns were hung in this steeple for about a minute on 18 April 1775, long enough to be seen across the water and not long enough to be caught.
stops.yiki: Revere did not hang the lanterns himself. That was Robert Newman, the sexton, who climbed the steeple and then slipped out a back window to get home unseen. Look up into the dark where he stood.

stops.name: Copp's Hill Burying Ground
stops.desc: The high ground the British used to shell Charlestown during Bunker Hill. Headstones here still carry musket damage from redcoats using them as targets.
stops.yiki: Walk to the far corner and look across the water. That rise is Charlestown and the monument you are heading for, so you can see the end of the walk from here. Many of Boston's free Black residents are buried in this ground.

stops.name: USS Constitution
stops.desc: Old Ironsides, launched 1797, still a commissioned Navy ship and the oldest warship afloat anywhere. Active duty sailors give the tours. Bring photo identification.

stops.name: Bunker Hill Monument
stops.desc: The end of the trail, and 294 steps with no lift. The battle was actually fought on Breed's Hill, the colonists lost, and it still convinced everyone the war was winnable.
stops.yiki: Two hundred and ninety four steps, and a small triumph at the top, since most people stop counting near two hundred. This is where they were told to hold their fire until they could see the whites of the enemy's eyes, because powder was too scarce to waste a shot.

trails.name: The National Mall
trails.summary: Two miles along one straight axis, from the Capitol and the Library of Congress across the road, west past the museums, up to the White House and its grey neighbour, then on to the Lincoln Memorial and round the Tidal Basin to Jefferson: twenty one stops, most of them free, and the only walk in the country where you can see the next monument from the one you are standing at. Distances are straight-line along the Mall's straight paths, marked as estimates, not routed.

stops.name: United States Capitol
stops.desc: The east end of the axis and the building everything else is measured from. The dome is cast iron painted to look like stone, and the Statue of Freedom on top faces east, away from the Mall.
stops.size_source: dc-form-capitol.js header, 288 ft to the Statue of Freedom's crest; OSM tags 87.6 m. Footprint from the OSM outline.

stops.name: Library of Congress
stops.desc: Across First Street from the Capitol, or under it through the pedestrian tunnel from the Visitor Center: the Jefferson Building of 1897, New Hampshire granite under a gilded torch, the Great Hall and the Main Reading Room. The walk doubles back west afterwards, so go now, not later.

stops.name: United States Botanic Garden
stops.desc: The oldest continually operating botanic garden in the country, in a conservatory at the foot of Capitol Hill. Free, warm, and the place to get out of the weather.

stops.name: National Museum of the American Indian
stops.desc: Curved limestone meant to read as wind-carved rock, the only museum on the Mall whose building refuses the axis. The cafe is the best on the Mall.
stops.size_source: dc-form-indian.js header: OSM lidar height 42 m; 80 by 40 m massing.

stops.name: National Air and Space Museum
stops.desc: The Wright Flyer, the Spirit of St. Louis and the Apollo 11 command module under one roof. Timed passes, free, and they go fast.
stops.size_source: dc-form-airspace.js header, 82 ft 9 in, with OSM relation 16159112 agreeing. Footprint from the OSM outline.

stops.name: National Gallery of Art
stops.desc: The West Building is the marble one, the East Building is the angles. Free, and the only Leonardo in the Americas is in the West.
stops.size_source: OSM height tag and building outline.

stops.name: Hirshhorn Museum
stops.desc: The concrete drum on legs, and the sculpture garden sunk beside it. Modern and contemporary, free, and the building is the first exhibit.
stops.size_source: dc-form-hirshhorn.js header citing Wikipedia: 82 ft (25 m) high, 231 ft (70 m) diameter. OSM's outline here is the plaza, not the drum.

stops.name: Smithsonian Castle
stops.desc: Red sandstone and towers, 1855, the Smithsonian's first building and its front door. Closed for renovation at the time of writing; the outside is the visit.

stops.name: National Museum of Natural History
stops.desc: The elephant in the rotunda, the Hope Diamond upstairs, and more visitors than any other museum on the Mall. Go early or go at four.
stops.size_source: OSM building:levels x 4 m and the building outline.

stops.name: National Museum of American History
stops.desc: The Star-Spangled Banner in a dark room, Dorothy's ruby slippers, and the flag that was the anthem. Free.

stops.name: National Museum of African American History and Culture
stops.desc: The bronze corona, three tiers widening as they rise, the newest museum on the Mall and the one that needs the most time. Timed passes, free.
stops.size_source: OSM height tag and building outline.

stops.name: The White House
stops.desc: Hoban's house of 1800, seen from the Ellipse: the south front with its six column bow and the Truman Balcony. Three floors on this side and two on the other, because the ground falls away. Free to look at, and inside only by a request made weeks ahead through Congress.
stops.yiki: This one is a real detour and it is worth knowing the cost: the museums to the Monument is a four minute walk, and going by the White House makes it about twenty two. It is 900 m off the Mall's axis, in President's Park, not on the Mall at all. Walk round to Pennsylvania Avenue for the four column portico everyone photographs, then come back down to the Monument. The east lawn is a construction site: the East Wing came down in October 2025 and the new State Ballroom is going up in its place. Check the Park Service page on the day, parts of President's Park have been closed through 2026 for security work.
stops.size_source: White House Historical Association: 70 ft high on the south, 168 ft long.

stops.name: Eisenhower Executive Office Building
stops.desc: The grey Second Empire block west of the White House, 1871 to 1888, home to the State, War and Navy departments: nine hundred columns, 1,572 windows, slate mansards. Seen from 17th Street; not open to walk into.

stops.name: Washington Monument
stops.desc: The tallest stone structure in the world, and the colour changes a third of the way up where construction stopped for twenty-two years. Tickets for the top are timed and free.
stops.size_source: dc-form-monument.js header: 555 ft to the apex, 55 ft square at the foot.

stops.name: World War II Memorial
stops.desc: Fifty-six pillars around the pool, one per state and territory, between the Monument and the Reflecting Pool. The Freedom Wall carries 4,048 gold stars, one for every hundred dead.
stops.size_source: dc-form-wwii.js header: two 43 ft (13 m) arches; plaza 337 ft 10 in (103 m) long.

stops.name: Vietnam Veterans Memorial
stops.desc: Two black granite arms sunk into the ground, 58,000 names in the order they died. Bring paper for a rubbing; the rangers have pencils.
stops.size_source: dc-form-vietnam.js header: 10.1 ft (3.1 m) tall at the apex; each wall 246 ft 9 in (75.2 m) long.

stops.name: Lincoln Memorial
stops.desc: Thirty-six columns for the states at Lincoln's death, and the step where King stood is marked. Best at dawn and after dark, when it is lit and the crowds are gone.
stops.size_source: dc-form-lincoln.js header, 99 ft foundation to roofline; 189 ft 8 in long.

stops.name: Korean War Veterans Memorial
stops.desc: Nineteen steel soldiers walking through juniper, and a black granite wall that reflects them into thirty-eight, for the parallel. Go at dusk.
stops.size_source: dc-form-korean.js header: mural wall approx 12 ft (3.7 m) high; 70 by 38 m field.

stops.name: Martin Luther King Jr. Memorial
stops.desc: The Stone of Hope pulled forward out of the Mountain of Despair, on the Tidal Basin between Lincoln and Jefferson, on a line that was chosen on purpose.

stops.name: Franklin Delano Roosevelt Memorial
stops.desc: Four outdoor rooms, one per term, with waterfalls, along the Tidal Basin. The only presidential memorial you walk through rather than up to.

stops.name: Jefferson Memorial
stops.desc: The rotunda across the water from the Monument, on axis with the White House. The cherry trees around it are the ones people come in April for.
stops.size_source: dc-form-jefferson.js header: overall height 129 ft (39 m), diameter 165 ft (50 m).

trails.name: Mount Rushmore
trails.summary: Eight stops around the memorial in walking order, from the Avenue of Flags to the base of the carving and back up past Borglum's studio. Under a mile on paved path, with 422 stairs on one side of the loop. No entrance fee, but parking is a concession charge and the America the Beautiful pass does not cover it.

stops.name: Avenue of Flags
stops.desc: Fifty six flags: fifty states, one district, three territories and two commonwealths. Put up in 1976 for the Bicentennial, at a visitor's suggestion. Walk between them and the faces are framed at the far end.
stops.yiki: Find your own flag on the way in. They are in alphabetical order, and the avenue is the one place at this memorial designed to be walked down rather than stood at.

stops.name: Grand View Terrace
stops.desc: The head-on view, and the one on every postcard. Each face is sixty feet from chin to hairline. Washington's is the only one carved with any detail below the chin, because the money ran out.
stops.yiki: The plan was heads to the waist. What stopped it was funding, not design, so what you are looking at is an unfinished sculpture that everyone has agreed to treat as finished.

stops.name: Lincoln Borglum Visitor Center
stops.desc: The museum under the terrace, named for the sculptor's son, who took over when his father died in March 1941 and finished the carving that October. Free.
stops.yiki: Go here before the trail, not after. The film and the models explain what you are about to walk under, and the trail is better when you know what the drill marks are.

stops.name: Presidential Trail
stops.desc: A 0.6 mile paved loop from the Grand View Terrace that takes you to the base of the mountain. The section down toward the Sculptor's Studio is 422 stairs, so the loop is one way round if steps are a problem.
stops.yiki: Walk it counter-clockwise. That puts the stairs going down rather than up, and it saves the closest viewpoint for last.

stops.name: Under the faces
stops.desc: The closest the public gets. From directly underneath the proportions stop working and you see it as what it is: a mountain with 450,000 tons blasted off it, about nine tenths of that by dynamite.
stops.yiki: Look for the talus, the rubble field below the carving. It was never cleared, and it is every ton that came off the faces, still lying where it fell.

stops.name: Lakota, Nakota and Dakota Heritage Village
stops.desc: On the Nature Trail below the studio. The Black Hills were granted to the Lakota in perpetuity by the 1868 Treaty of Fort Laramie and taken back after 1876. The mountain's older name is Tȟuŋkášila Šákpe, the Six Grandfathers.
stops.yiki: In 1980 the Supreme Court ruled the Sioux had never received just compensation for the Black Hills. The award has been refused and sits uncollected, because taking it would be accepting payment for land never agreed to be sold.

stops.name: Sculptor's Studio
stops.desc: Gutzon Borglum's working studio, with the plaster model the carving was measured from. Ranger talks run here through the season.
stops.yiki: The model is one twelfth scale. Every point on the mountain was transferred from it by a pointing machine, a boom and a plumb line, which is how you carve a face sixty feet tall and get the eyes right.

stops.name: Evening Lighting Ceremony
stops.desc: In the amphitheater below the terrace, nightly from the Friday of Memorial Day weekend to the end of September. It is the best attended ranger programme in the entire National Park Service.
stops.yiki: Come back for it rather than trying to fit it into the same visit. The faces lit against a dark mountain are a different sight from the daytime one, and the amphitheater fills early in July and August.

trails.name: Harvard, the Yard and around it
trails.summary: Ten stops in and around Harvard Yard, the oldest college ground in the country: from the T stop through Johnston Gate, past the statue everyone rubs, to the library a mother built for a son lost on the Titanic, and out to the museums. About a mile. Distances are straight lines, marked as estimates.

stops.name: Harvard Square
stops.desc: The T stop, the newsstand, the Coop and the crowds: the town side of the wall. Everything on this walk is within ten minutes of this spot.
stops.yiki: Start here, on the town side of the wall. Look at the brick wall across Massachusetts Avenue and find a gate in it. That is where the university begins.

stops.name: Johnston Gate
stops.desc: The main gate into Harvard Yard, 1889, brick and wrought iron by McKim, Mead and White, the first of the gates that turned an open green into an enclosed yard.
stops.yiki: Read the panels either side before you go through. One carries the 1636 vote that founded the college, the other the reason the founders gave for it.

stops.name: Massachusetts Hall
stops.desc: Harvard's oldest building, finished in 1720, brick and plain. Washington's troops were quartered in it in 1775. The president's office is on the ground floor and first-year students still live upstairs.
stops.yiki: Look at the top floor windows. Students live behind them, in the oldest college building still in use in the country, above the president's office.

stops.name: John Harvard Statue
stops.desc: Daniel Chester French's seated bronze of 1884 in front of University Hall, the most photographed object in Cambridge. Its inscription is famous for being wrong three times: the face is a student's, John Harvard was a benefactor not the founder, and the college dates to 1636, not 1638.
stops.yiki: Everyone rubs the left shoe for luck. Look at the inscription instead and count the errors: the face, the word founder, the year. Three, on one plinth.

stops.name: Memorial Church
stops.desc: The white spire on the north side of the Yard, 1932, built for the Harvard dead of the First World War. Their names are cut into the walls of the Memorial Room inside, with the dead of later wars added.
stops.yiki: Go in if the door is open and find the Memorial Room. The names are cut into the wall, by war, and the room is the reason the church exists.

stops.name: Widener Library
stops.desc: The great flight of steps and the columns on the south side of the Yard, 1915. Eleanor Elkins Widener built it for her son Harry, a book collector who died on the Titanic, and gave it his collection. The largest university library building in the world.
stops.yiki: Stand at the bottom of the steps and look up. Then turn round: the church faces you across the grass, and this pairing is the picture of Harvard everyone carries.

stops.name: Sever Hall
stops.desc: H. H. Richardson's brick classroom building of 1880, a National Historic Landmark, with carved brick ornament and a famous whispering arch at the west door.
stops.yiki: Find the arched entrance on the Yard side. Stand facing the brick on one side of the arch and have someone whisper into the other side. It carries.

stops.name: Harvard Art Museums
stops.desc: Three museums under one glass roof by Renzo Piano, 2014: the Fogg, the Busch-Reisinger and the Sackler, with the Straus conservation labs visible from the top floor.
stops.yiki: Go up to the top floor first and look down through the glass at the courtyard, then work your way down. The conservation labs are behind the glass up there.

stops.name: Memorial Hall
stops.desc: The red Gothic pile north of the Yard, 1878, built to the Harvard dead of the Union side of the Civil War. Sanders Theatre is in the east end, the transept holds the names, and Annenberg Hall, the first-year dining hall, is the nave.
stops.yiki: The transept between the theatre and the dining hall is the memorial, with the names on the walls. Ask at the door; it is usually open even when the hall is not.

stops.name: Harvard Science Center
stops.desc: Josep Lluis Sert's stepped concrete building of 1973 on the north edge of the Yard, said to be shaped like a camera, with the Cabot Science Library inside and the plaza in front where the food trucks park.
stops.yiki: Turn round here and look back through the Yard. You have crossed the whole of the old college in a few hundred metres, and the town is on the other side.

trails.name: Yale, from the Old Campus to the libraries
trails.summary: Ten stops through the Collegiate Gothic heart of Yale: in by Phelps Gate, round the Old Campus and its 1750s hall, up Harkness Tower, across to Louis Kahn's two art museums, then north past the Sterling library to the marble box of the Beinecke. Under a mile.

stops.name: Phelps Gate
stops.desc: The archway from the New Haven Green into the Old Campus, under Phelps Hall of 1896. Every Yale student walks in through it in their first week and out through it at Commencement.
stops.yiki: Walk through the arch slowly. In four years a student goes through it twice on purpose, in and out, and thousands of times without noticing.

stops.name: Connecticut Hall
stops.desc: The oldest building at Yale, brick, finished in 1752, and the only one left of the old brick row. Nathan Hale lived in it as a student; his statue stands outside.
stops.yiki: Find the statue of Nathan Hale by the door and look at his hands and feet. He is tied. He was hanged as a spy at twenty one.

stops.name: Old Campus
stops.desc: The quadrangle of first-year dormitories, elm trees and paths, where the college lived for its first two centuries. The statue of Theodore Dwight Woolsey, president in the 1850s, sits with a bright toe.
stops.yiki: Sit on a bench for five minutes. This is where first years live, and in September the courtyard is the busiest place in New Haven.

stops.name: Harkness Tower
stops.desc: James Gamble Rogers's 216 foot Gothic tower of 1921, the tallest thing on campus, with a carillon of 54 bells that plays most evenings. Part of Memorial Quadrangle, now Branford and Saybrook colleges.
stops.yiki: Stand back on High Street until you can see the whole tower. It was built to look old the year it was finished, and the stone was distressed by hand to help.

stops.name: Yale University Art Gallery
stops.desc: The oldest university art museum in the country, 1832, in three joined buildings, the newest Louis Kahn's of 1953, his first major work. Van Gogh's Night Cafe is here, and Trumbull's paintings of the Revolution.
stops.yiki: Go straight to the Kahn building and look up at the concrete ceiling, a grid of tetrahedra. Then find the Night Cafe. Both are on the same visit and both are free.

stops.name: Yale Center for British Art
stops.desc: Louis Kahn's last building, finished in 1977 after his death, across Chapel Street from his first. Steel, concrete, white oak and travertine around two courtyards, holding the largest collection of British art outside Britain. Free.
stops.yiki: Cross the street and you cross Kahn's whole career, first building to last. Go in and stand in the entrance court and look up four floors.

stops.name: Cross Campus
stops.desc: The lawn between the Old Campus and the Sterling library, with the Bass Library under it. The Women's Table by Maya Lin, a granite fountain, counts the women enrolled at Yale each year from 1701.
stops.yiki: Find the Women's Table, the low granite oval with water on it. Read the numbers in the spiral. They start at zero and stay there for a long time.

stops.name: Sterling Memorial Library
stops.desc: A cathedral for books, 1930, James Gamble Rogers: the nave is the entrance hall, the circulation desk is the altar, and the tower behind holds fifteen storeys of stacks.
stops.yiki: Go in as far as the desk. The building was designed as a church and it makes no secret of it; look for the painted Alma Mater where the altarpiece would be.

stops.name: Beinecke Rare Book and Manuscript Library
stops.desc: Gordon Bunshaft's windowless marble box of 1963. The walls are Vermont marble an inch and a quarter thick, thin enough to glow amber inside. A Gutenberg Bible and an Audubon are on show in the glass tower of books.
stops.yiki: Go in and stand still for a moment. The light through the marble is the whole point of the building, and it changes with the weather outside.

stops.name: Woolsey Hall
stops.desc: The 1901 concert hall at the corner of Grove and College, with the Newberry organ inside and the rotunda entrance whose walls carry the names of Yale's war dead.
stops.yiki: Walk into the rotunda and read a few names on the marble. Then turn and look at the size of the hall. This is where the university gathers.

trails.name: Princeton, Nassau Hall to the Chapel
trails.summary: Eleven stops from the town square through FitzRandolph Gate to Nassau Hall, the building that was the capital of the United States for four months in 1783, then round Cannon Green, the Chapel, Firestone Library, the house Woodrow Wilson lived in, the new art museum and the Gothic arches on the west side. About a mile.

stops.name: Palmer Square
stops.desc: The town's green, laid out in the 1930s opposite the campus gate, with the shops and the Nassau Inn round it. Nassau Street, the town's main street, is the line between Princeton the town and Princeton the university.
stops.yiki: Cross Nassau Street and you cross from town to gown. Look at the gate before you go through it; it is the only formal front door the university has.

stops.name: FitzRandolph Gate
stops.desc: The iron gate on Nassau Street, 1905, named for the family that gave the land. Closed for most of its life; the class of 1970 asked for it to be opened permanently, and it has been. Students avoid walking out through it before they graduate.
stops.yiki: Go in through the centre gate. Students will not walk OUT through it until Commencement, so if you see someone step round it, that is why.

stops.name: Nassau Hall
stops.desc: 1756, the largest stone building in the colonies when it was built, named for William of Orange. It was the whole college for decades, took cannon fire in the Battle of Princeton in 1777, and housed the Continental Congress from June to November 1783, which makes it a former capital of the United States.
stops.yiki: Look for the cannonball scar on the wall by the west end, and the bronze tigers either side of the door. Then remember Congress met upstairs.

stops.name: Cannon Green
stops.desc: The lawn behind Nassau Hall with a Revolutionary War cannon buried muzzle down in the middle, the prize in a long feud with Rutgers, who stole it once.
stops.yiki: The cannon is buried so nobody can steal it again. Find it, and the second one over by Whig Hall that Rutgers tried for instead.

stops.name: East Pyne Hall and Chancellor Green
stops.desc: Two of the older buildings east of Nassau Hall: Chancellor Green, the octagonal library of 1873 with a stained glass dome, now a cafe and reading room, and East Pyne, the courtyard building of 1897 with statues of the college's early presidents.
stops.yiki: Go into Chancellor Green and look up at the dome. It was the library. Then walk through East Pyne's courtyard, which is the best small courtyard on campus.

stops.name: Firestone Library
stops.desc: The main library, 1948, mostly underground: more floors of stacks below the lawn than the Gothic building above shows. Its special collections hold F. Scott Fitzgerald's papers.
stops.yiki: Look at the lawn beside it. You are standing on the library; most of it is under your feet.

stops.name: Princeton University Chapel
stops.desc: Ralph Adams Cram's Gothic chapel of 1928, one of the largest university chapels in the world, with a nave of 250 feet and glass by the leading American studios of the day.
stops.yiki: Go in, sit at the back, and give your eyes a minute. Then walk the nave and count the steps. It is longer than it looks from outside.

stops.name: Prospect House
stops.desc: The Italianate villa of 1850s in the middle of campus, the president's house from 1878 to 1968. Woodrow Wilson lived here as president and his wife Ellen laid out the flower garden behind it. Now the faculty club.
stops.yiki: Walk round to the garden at the back. Ellen Wilson designed it, and it is the one place on campus that is deliberately not Gothic.

stops.name: Princeton University Art Museum
stops.desc: The university's museum, free, with a collection from ancient China to Warhol. A new building by David Adjaye replaced the old one on this site; check the museum's own page for current hours and what is on view.
stops.yiki: Ask at the desk for whatever is newest, then go and find the antiquities. Most people come for the modern rooms and leave the old ones empty.

stops.name: Blair Hall and Blair Arch
stops.desc: The first Collegiate Gothic dormitory at Princeton, 1897, with the great arch and steps that once led down to the railway station. The trains stopped here until the station moved.
stops.yiki: Stand at the top of the steps inside the arch and look down. Students arrived by train at the bottom and climbed straight into college through this arch.

stops.name: Alexander Hall
stops.desc: The Romanesque auditorium of 1894, brownstone and granite with a carved frieze across the front, Richardson's manner a decade after Richardson. Richardson Auditorium inside seats the university's concerts.
stops.yiki: Walk round to the front and look at the carving. It was the least popular building on campus for a century and is now one of the most loved.

trails.name: Columbia, the Morningside campus
trails.summary: Ten stops on McKim, Mead and White's campus of 1897 in Morningside Heights: in from Broadway along College Walk, up the steps to Alma Mater and Low Library, down to Butler, the sundial, the two halls that made the news, the Thinker, and north to the physics building where the atomic age began. Half a mile, all of it inside the campus gates.

stops.name: College Walk
stops.desc: 116th Street between Broadway and Amsterdam, closed to traffic and turned into the campus's main axis. The gates at each end are the way in.
stops.yiki: Come in from Broadway. Stop halfway along the walk and look left, up the steps, and right, down at Butler. The whole campus is that one view.

stops.name: Alma Mater
stops.desc: Daniel Chester French's bronze of 1903 on the steps of Low Library, the seated figure with her arms open. The owl hidden in her robe is the thing students are told to find.
stops.yiki: Find the owl. It is tucked in the folds of her gown on the left side. Then sit on the steps; they are the campus's sofa.

stops.name: Low Memorial Library
stops.desc: McKim's domed centrepiece of 1897, granite, with the largest all-granite dome in the country. A library for only a few decades; now the administration, with the Visitors Center inside.
stops.yiki: Go up the steps and in. The rotunda under the dome is open and almost always empty, and it is the one room on campus built to impress.

stops.name: Butler Library
stops.desc: The main library, 1934, facing Low across the lawns, with the names of the ancient authors carved along the frieze. Homer, Herodotus, Sophocles, Plato, and so on, in the order a classicist would put them.
stops.yiki: Read the frieze from left to right. Then notice what is missing from it, which is any name from after the fall of Rome.

stops.name: The Sundial
stops.desc: The granite base in the middle of College Walk that carried a sixteen-ton green granite sphere from 1885 until 1946, when the sphere cracked and was removed. The base is a speakers' platform now.
stops.yiki: Stand on it. This is where speeches on this campus are given, and have been since the sphere came off.

stops.name: Hamilton Hall
stops.desc: The Columbia College building of 1907 with the statue of Alexander Hamilton outside, class of 1778. Occupied by students in 1968 and again in 2024.
stops.yiki: Look at the statue, then at the doors. Both dates that made this building famous happened on the other side of them.

stops.name: Philosophy Hall
stops.desc: The 1910 building on the east side of campus with a cast of Rodin's Thinker outside the door. FM radio was worked out inside it by Edwin Armstrong in the 1930s.
stops.yiki: Sit with the Thinker for a moment. He was cast from Rodin's own moulds. Then read the plaque about FM radio by the door.

stops.name: Avery Hall
stops.desc: Home of the architecture school and the Avery Architectural and Fine Arts Library, the largest architecture library in the country.
stops.yiki: If the library lets you in, go down a floor and look at the drawings on display. If not, the reading room door is worth a glance.

stops.name: Earl Hall
stops.desc: The domed building of 1902 on the west side of Low, built for religious and student life, and the home of the university's chaplaincies.
stops.yiki: Notice the dome, a small echo of Low's. McKim's plan has echoes everywhere once you start seeing them.

stops.name: Pupin Hall
stops.desc: The physics building of 1927 at the north end of campus. Here in 1939 the uranium atom was split in the United States for the first time, and the work that became the Manhattan Project began. A National Historic Landmark.
stops.yiki: This is the end of the walk and the beginning of the atomic age. The experiment was in the basement. Read the plaque, and think about the date on it.

trails.name: Penn, along Locust Walk
trails.summary: Ten stops along Locust Walk, the spine of the University of Pennsylvania: from the bench where Benjamin Franklin sits with a newspaper to the Split Button, College Hall, Frank Furness's library and the museum with the largest sphinx in the western hemisphere. Under a mile, all on the campus paths.

stops.name: Benjamin Franklin on a bench
stops.desc: George Lundeen's bronze of 1987 at 37th and Locust: Franklin on a park bench reading a newspaper, with room beside him. The founder of the university, sitting in the middle of it.
stops.yiki: Sit next to him. Everyone does. Then look down Locust Walk, because the whole campus is laid out along it from here.

stops.name: Locust Walk
stops.desc: The brick path that replaced Locust Street through the campus in the 1960s, lined with the older houses and halls, the way every student gets to class.
stops.yiki: Walk it slowly. It is a street with the cars taken out, and the buildings on it are older than the walk.

stops.name: The Split Button
stops.desc: Claes Oldenburg's sixteen-foot aluminium button of 1981 in front of Van Pelt Library, split in the middle. The joke is on the statue of Franklin nearby, whose waistcoat could have lost it.
stops.yiki: Look for the four holes and the split. Then look for Franklin. Oldenburg said the button popped off him.

stops.name: Van Pelt-Dietrich Library
stops.desc: The main library, 1962, with the rare books on the top floor and Franklin's own reading chair upstairs among the university's founding papers.
stops.yiki: Card access for the stacks, but the ground floor and the exhibition cases are open. Ask about the Kislak Center on the sixth floor.

stops.name: College Green and the Franklin statue
stops.desc: The lawn in front of College Hall with John Boyle's standing bronze of Franklin, 1899, moved here from City Hall in 1939.
stops.yiki: Two Franklins in five minutes: this one standing, the other on his bench. The university has more statues of him than anyone.

stops.name: College Hall
stops.desc: The first building on the West Philadelphia campus, 1873, in green serpentine stone that has been weathering ever since. Said to be one of the models for the Addams Family house.
stops.yiki: Look at the colour of the stone. Serpentine, green, and softer than it should be; the university has been repairing it for a century.

stops.name: Houston Hall
stops.desc: The first student union in the country, 1896, still the students' building: food, meeting rooms, a great hall with a fireplace.
stops.yiki: Go in. It is open to anyone, and the hall on the ground floor is where the idea of a student union was invented.

stops.name: Irvine Auditorium
stops.desc: The Gothic pile of 1932 at 34th and Spruce with the Curtis Organ inside, one of the largest organs in the world, built for the 1926 Sesquicentennial exposition.
stops.yiki: Look up at the roofline. The building was designed to be seen from above; the organ inside was designed to be heard from anywhere.

stops.name: Fisher Fine Arts Library
stops.desc: Frank Furness's red sandstone library of 1891, a National Historic Landmark, with a four-storey reading room under a skylight and the stacks in a glass and iron tower behind. Louis Kahn taught here and loved it.
stops.yiki: Go in and stand in the reading room and look up. Furness built a library like a factory and a cathedral at once, and it was nearly demolished in the 1960s.

stops.name: Penn Museum
stops.desc: The University of Pennsylvania Museum of Archaeology and Anthropology, 1899, with the Sphinx of Ramses II, the largest sphinx in the western hemisphere, the Royal Tombs of Ur, and the Chinese rotunda.
stops.yiki: Go to the sphinx first. It is in the entrance hall now, twelve tons of red granite from Memphis, and it was buried to the shoulders when it was found.

trails.name: Brown, through the Van Wickle Gates
trails.summary: Eleven stops on College Hill: in through the gates that open twice a year, past the 1770 hall and the chapel, up the tower, into the two great libraries, across the green to the campus centre and out to the science library. Half a mile on the hill above Providence.

stops.name: Van Wickle Gates
stops.desc: The wrought iron gates on Prospect Street, 1901. Opened inward once a year for the new class in September and outward once for the graduates in May; walking through them any other time is said to bring bad luck.
stops.yiki: Do not walk through the middle gate. Students will not, and they will tell you why. The side gates are fine.

stops.name: University Hall
stops.desc: The oldest building at Brown, brick, 1770, the whole college for its first decades and a barracks and hospital for French and American troops in the Revolution. A National Historic Landmark.
stops.yiki: Look at the brick. The building was the college, entirely, when it was built, and it has been the president's office ever since.

stops.name: Manning Hall
stops.desc: The Greek Revival chapel of 1834, a Doric temple twice the size of its model at Paestum, now the university's chapel.
stops.yiki: Count the columns on the front: four, Doric, and the whole building is a doubled Greek temple.

stops.name: Carrie Tower
stops.desc: The brick and stone clock tower of 1904 at the corner of the green, built by Paul Bajnotti of Turin for his wife Carrie, a Brown family granddaughter. Love is strong as death, says the inscription.
stops.yiki: Read the inscription at the base. The man who built it was Italian and built two memorials to her in this city; the other is the fountain downtown.

stops.name: John Hay Library
stops.desc: The marble library of 1910, named for Lincoln's secretary, and the home of the special collections: the Lincoln papers, the H. P. Lovecraft papers, and a collection of toy soldiers.
stops.yiki: Ask at the desk about the Lovecraft collection. He lived a few streets away and the library holds his manuscripts.

stops.name: John D. Rockefeller Jr. Library
stops.desc: The main library, 1964, brick and glass, called the Rock, with the study spaces students live in during exams.
stops.yiki: Look at how it faces University Hall across the road: the 1960s bowing to the 1770s.

stops.name: Sayles Hall
stops.desc: The Romanesque hall of 1881 with the portraits of every president and the Hutchings-Votey organ, played at midnight before Halloween.
stops.yiki: Go in if it is open and look at the portraits down both walls. Every president of the university since 1765 is watching you.

stops.name: John Carter Brown Library
stops.desc: The 1904 Beaux-Arts library on the green holding one of the world's great collections of early Americana: books and maps printed before 1825 about the Americas.
stops.yiki: Go in and look at whatever map is on show. The collection is the reason people fly to Providence.

stops.name: Faunce House
stops.desc: The 1904 student union, now the Stephen Robert Campus Center, with the Blue Room cafe and the arch students walk through to the green.
stops.yiki: Go through the arch to the green and turn round. The arch frames the whole main green behind you.

stops.name: Soldiers Memorial Gate
stops.desc: The brick and limestone gate of 1921 at the top of Lincoln Field, the memorial to the Brown men who died in the First World War.
stops.yiki: Read the names in the arch, then look down the playing field. The field is the memorial too.

stops.name: Sciences Library
stops.desc: The fourteen-storey concrete tower of 1971, the SciLi, the tallest building on College Hill and the view from the top of Thayer Street.
stops.yiki: Look up. It is the one building on this hill that does not pretend to be old, and students love it for exactly that.

trails.name: Dartmouth, round the Green
trails.summary: Eleven stops round the Green in Hanover, the smallest Ivy and the one that still looks like a New England village: the inn, the row of white halls, the chapel, the library with the Orozco murals, the house with afternoon tea, the arts centre that was a rehearsal for Lincoln Center, and the museum. Half a mile, flat, and the Green is the middle of everything.

stops.name: Hanover Inn
stops.desc: The college's own hotel on the south side of the Green, on the site of a tavern that has served the college since the 1780s.
stops.yiki: Start on the inn's front steps. Everything on this walk is visible from here, round one lawn.

stops.name: Dartmouth Green
stops.desc: The five-acre lawn in the middle of the college and the town, cleared of pines in the 1770s, where the bonfire is built every autumn and the snow sculpture every winter.
stops.yiki: Walk to the middle and turn a full circle. Library, halls, chapel, inn, town. This is the whole college in one turn.

stops.name: Dartmouth Hall and Dartmouth Row
stops.desc: The white clapboard row on the east side of the Green: Dartmouth Hall of 1784, burned and rebuilt in brick painted white in 1906, with Wentworth and Thornton either side. The picture of the college.
stops.yiki: Stand across the Green and look at the three white halls in a row. That is the image the college uses for everything, and it is real.

stops.name: Rollins Chapel
stops.desc: The Romanesque chapel of 1885, granite and brownstone, now used for services of many faiths and for concerts.
stops.yiki: Go in if the door is open. The wooden ceiling is the thing to see.

stops.name: Webster Hall and Rauner Library
stops.desc: Webster Hall of 1907, named for Daniel Webster, class of 1801, converted in 2000 into the Rauner Special Collections Library, which holds the college's charter of 1769 and the Robert Frost papers.
stops.yiki: Ask to see whatever is on display. The charter is here, and the staff are used to visitors who only want to look.

stops.name: Baker Library and the Orozco murals
stops.desc: The 1928 library with the bell tower modelled on Independence Hall, and in its reserve reading room downstairs the Epic of American Civilization, twenty-four fresco panels painted by Jose Clemente Orozco between 1932 and 1934, a National Historic Landmark.
stops.yiki: Go downstairs to the reading room and walk the murals from left to right. They are the reason to come to Hanover, and they are free.

stops.name: Sanborn House
stops.desc: The 1929 English department building with a panelled library where tea is served every weekday afternoon at four, a tradition since the building opened.
stops.yiki: If it is four o'clock on a weekday, go in. Tea and a cookie for a few cents, in a room that has not changed since 1929.

stops.name: Parkhurst Hall
stops.desc: The administration building of 1911 on the west side of the Green, the president's office, occupied by students in the protest of 1969.
stops.yiki: Look at the doors. The college's most famous argument was held on the other side of them.

stops.name: Collis Center
stops.desc: The student centre, built round College Hall of 1901, with the cafe and common rooms where the campus eats between classes.
stops.yiki: Go in for coffee. This is the college's living room, and nobody will mind.

stops.name: Hopkins Center for the Arts
stops.desc: Wallace Harrison's arts centre of 1962, with the arched glass front. Harrison designed it before the Metropolitan Opera House at Lincoln Center, which it resembles for a reason.
stops.yiki: Look at the arched windows on the front, then think of the Met Opera in New York. Same architect, this one first.

stops.name: Hood Museum of Art
stops.desc: The college museum, Charles Moore's building of 1985 expanded by Tod Williams and Billie Tsien in 2019, with Assyrian reliefs from Nimrud among the oldest objects in any American college collection.
stops.yiki: Find the Assyrian reliefs. They came to Hanover in 1856 and they are older than almost anything else in New England.

trails.name: Cornell, the Arts Quad and the slope
trails.summary: Eleven stops on the hill above Cayuga Lake: from the student union to the chapel where the founders are buried, up the clock tower whose chimes play three times a day, along the top of Libe Slope, round the Arts Quad past the two founders' statues and the first building, to the president's house and the museum I. M. Pei built on the edge of the gorge. About a mile, with one climb.

stops.name: Willard Straight Hall
stops.desc: The student union of 1925, on Ho Plaza, the campus's meeting place. Taken over by armed students in 1969 in the protest that made the cover of Newsweek.
stops.yiki: Start on the plaza in front. The tower is up the path to your right and the lake is behind you, down the slope.

stops.name: Sage Chapel
stops.desc: The 1875 chapel with the mosaic apse, where Ezra Cornell and Andrew Dickson White, the founders, are buried in the memorial antechapel.
stops.yiki: Go in and turn left into the small room off the entrance. The founders are here, both of them, under the mosaics.

stops.name: McGraw Tower
stops.desc: The 173-foot clock tower of 1891 with the Cornell Chimes, twenty-one bells played by students three times a day, and 161 steps to the top.
stops.yiki: Climb it at chime time if you can, morning, noon or evening. The players let you stand in the room while the bells go.

stops.name: Uris Library and Libe Slope
stops.desc: The 1891 library beside the tower with the A. D. White reading room, the one that looks like a Victorian dream of a library. Libe Slope falls away from the front door down to West Campus and the lake view.
stops.yiki: Go in and find the A. D. White Library, the wrought iron balconies. Then go out the front and sit on the slope at sunset, which is what everyone does.

stops.name: Ezra Cornell statue
stops.desc: The bronze of the founder of 1919 on the Arts Quad, facing his co-founder across the grass. Legend says the two statues meet at midnight when a virgin walks between them.
stops.yiki: Look across the quad to the other statue. Ezra built the telegraph fortune; White built the university with it. They are placed to see each other.

stops.name: Morrill Hall
stops.desc: The first building on campus, 1868, grey stone, named for the senator whose land-grant act paid for the university.
stops.yiki: This was the whole university once: classrooms, dormitory, offices. Look along the row of stone halls it started.

stops.name: Andrew Dickson White statue
stops.desc: The seated bronze of the first president, 1915, on the east side of the Arts Quad, facing Ezra Cornell.
stops.yiki: Sit on the bench near him and read the inscription. He wanted a university where any person could find instruction in any study, and the line is on everything.

stops.name: Goldwin Smith Hall
stops.desc: The Beaux-Arts arts building of 1906 behind White's statue, home of the humanities and of the Temple of Zeus cafe, named for the plaster casts that used to stand in it.
stops.yiki: Go in and find the cafe. The casts are gone but the name stayed, which is very Cornell.

stops.name: Andrew Dickson White House
stops.desc: The first president's own house of 1871, brick and Gothic, now the Society for the Humanities, with the library he built inside.
stops.yiki: Walk round it. White designed the university and this house at the same time, and the house is the smaller version of the idea.

stops.name: Johnson Museum of Art
stops.desc: I. M. Pei's concrete museum of 1973 on the edge of Fall Creek gorge, nicknamed the sewing machine, with a fifth-floor gallery of Asian art and the best view of the lake on campus.
stops.yiki: Take the lift to the fifth floor first. The Asian art is up there, and so is the window over the lake.

stops.name: Sibley Hall
stops.desc: The domed building of the 1870s at the north end of the Arts Quad, home of the architecture school, with the Fine Arts Library under the dome.
stops.yiki: End under the dome. Then find the path behind it to the suspension bridge over the gorge, which is the other thing Cornell is famous for.

trails.name: Philadelphia, Independence Hall to the Art Museum
trails.summary: Nineteen stops across the city where the country was written: the Liberty Bell and Independence Hall, the halls where Congress and the Supreme Court first sat, Franklin's court and Christ Church, the oldest street of houses, then west through the market and City Hall and up the Parkway to the Rocky steps and the prison that invented solitary confinement. About four miles; the Parkway half can be done by bus.

stops.name: Independence Visitor Center
stops.desc: The Park Service's front desk for the whole historic district, on Independence Mall. Timed tickets for Independence Hall are issued here in the morning.
stops.yiki: Come here first. Get the Independence Hall ticket before you do anything else, because they run out.

stops.name: Liberty Bell Center
stops.desc: The bell, cast in London in 1752, recast twice in Philadelphia, cracked beyond repair by 1846, and the words on it from Leviticus that the abolitionists made famous. Free, with an exhibition on the way in.
stops.yiki: Read the crack from the bottom up. The famous split is the wide one; the hairline above it is the one that finally silenced it.

stops.name: Independence Hall
stops.desc: The Pennsylvania State House, finished in 1753, where the Declaration of Independence was adopted in July 1776 and the Constitution signed in September 1787. A World Heritage Site. Rangers take you into the Assembly Room.
stops.yiki: In the Assembly Room, find Washington's chair with the sun carved on the back. Franklin watched it through the whole convention and decided at the end it was rising.

stops.name: Congress Hall
stops.desc: The county courthouse of 1789 next door, which housed the Congress of the United States from 1790 to 1800 while Philadelphia was the capital. Washington's second inauguration and Adams's first were here.
stops.yiki: Upstairs is the Senate, downstairs the House. Stand in the House and imagine sixty five men and a fireplace.

stops.name: Old City Hall
stops.desc: The 1791 city hall on the other side of Independence Hall, which housed the Supreme Court of the United States for its first decade.
stops.yiki: Three buildings in a row: the Congress, the Constitution, the Court. Nowhere else in the country are the three branches this close together.

stops.name: Second Bank of the United States
stops.desc: William Strickland's marble Greek temple of 1824, the Parthenon on Chestnut Street, and the portrait gallery inside with Charles Willson Peale's paintings of the founders from life.
stops.yiki: Go in and find Peale's portraits. These are the faces as they were, painted by a man who knew them, not the ones on the money.

stops.name: Carpenters' Hall
stops.desc: The guild hall of 1774 where the First Continental Congress met in September that year, still owned by the Carpenters' Company that built it.
stops.yiki: Stand in the room. The delegates met here because the State House belonged to the colony, and this belonged to nobody but the carpenters.

stops.name: Museum of the American Revolution
stops.desc: Opened 2017 on Third Street, with Washington's actual headquarters tent at the end of the visit, shown in a short film before the curtain rises on it.
stops.yiki: Do not skip the tent at the end. It is the real one, the canvas he slept under for years, and the film before it is short.

stops.name: Franklin Court and the Benjamin Franklin Museum
stops.desc: The site of Franklin's house, marked by Robert Venturi's steel ghost frame of 1976, with the museum underground, the working print shop, and the post office he founded still selling stamps.
stops.yiki: Stand inside the steel outline and look down through the portals at the foundations. The house is gone; the frame draws it in the air where it was.

stops.name: Christ Church
stops.desc: The Georgian church of 1727 to 1744 whose 1754 steeple made it the tallest building in the colonies for fifty years. Washington, Franklin and Betsy Ross had pews. Franklin is buried in the churchyard up the street.
stops.yiki: Find the Washington pew, marked, and then walk up to the burial ground on Arch Street and find Franklin under the pennies.

stops.name: Betsy Ross House
stops.desc: The small brick house on Arch Street where Betsy Ross, upholsterer, is said to have sewn the first stars and stripes in 1776. The story came from her grandson a century later; the house is real.
stops.yiki: The house is tiny and the stairs are steep. Notice how small a Philadelphia house was in 1776, whatever you decide about the flag.

stops.name: Elfreth's Alley
stops.desc: Thirty-two houses on a lane off Second Street, lived in since 1703, the oldest continuously inhabited residential street in the country. Two are a museum; the rest are homes.
stops.yiki: Walk to the end and back. People live here. Look at the busybody mirrors on the upper windows, so a woman could see who was at the door without going down.

stops.name: National Constitution Center
stops.desc: The museum of the Constitution at the north end of Independence Mall, 2003, with the live show that opens every visit and the hall of bronze signers you can stand among.
stops.yiki: In Signers' Hall, find the one man who refused to sign, and the delegate who was not there. Both are in bronze.

stops.name: Reading Terminal Market
stops.desc: The public market of 1892 under the old railway shed at 12th and Arch, open six days a week: Amish stands, cheesesteaks, roast pork, the Dutch Eating Place, and the best lunch in the city.
stops.yiki: Get in the roast pork line, not the cheesesteak line. Then find the Amish stands at the west end; they are only here Wednesday to Saturday.

stops.name: Philadelphia City Hall
stops.desc: The largest city hall in the country, 1871 to 1901, Second Empire, with the 37 foot bronze of William Penn on top of a 548 foot tower. By a gentlemen's agreement nothing in the city was built taller until 1987. The tower has an observation deck under Penn's feet.
stops.yiki: Stand in the courtyard in the middle and look straight up. Then go up the tower; the lift stops under the statue's feet.

stops.name: LOVE Park
stops.desc: JFK Plaza at the start of the Parkway, with Robert Indiana's LOVE sculpture of 1976 and the view straight up the Parkway to the Art Museum.
stops.yiki: Stand behind the sculpture and look up the Parkway. The museum is at the end, and everything between here and there was planned to be seen from this spot.

stops.name: Rodin Museum
stops.desc: The largest collection of Rodin outside Paris, in a small Beaux-Arts pavilion and garden of 1929 on the Parkway, with the Thinker at the gate and the Gates of Hell at the door.
stops.yiki: Look at the Gates of Hell for a full minute before you go in. The Thinker at the gate is a figure from it, made big.

stops.name: Philadelphia Museum of Art and the Rocky Steps
stops.desc: The Greek temple on the hill at the end of the Parkway, 1928, with 72 steps that Rocky ran up in 1976 and the statue of him at the bottom. Inside, one of the great collections: Duchamp, Cezanne's Large Bathers, the medieval cloister, the Japanese teahouse.
stops.yiki: Run the steps if you must; everybody does. Then go inside, because the collection is the reason the steps exist.

stops.name: Eastern State Penitentiary
stops.desc: The prison of 1829 that invented solitary confinement and was copied by three hundred prisons worldwide, closed in 1971 and left to decay. Al Capone's cell is furnished as he had it.
stops.yiki: Take the audio tour, narrated by Steve Buscemi, and stand in an empty cell with the door shut for one minute.

trails.name: The Ivy League, eight campuses
trails.summary: Eight universities, eight cities, one idea: the oldest colleges in the country and the towns that grew up round them. Each campus is its own walking tour in its own city, from Harvard's Yard in Cambridge to Cornell's gorges in Ithaca, and this page holds all eight. Pick a campus, or walk them in the order the colleges were founded.
